title: Personalized Recommendation System
summary: Retrieve and rank useful items while balancing relevance, discovery, inventory health, safety, and feedback loops.
prompt: Design a personalized recommendation system for a consumer home surface with a large and changing catalog.
clarifyingQuestions: Which surface, inventory, action, and session context define the recommendation?
How fresh must items and user signals be, and which items are ineligible?
productGoal: Reduce discovery effort while protecting satisfaction, safety, diversity, and catalog health.
predictionTarget: Rank eligible user-item candidates for a qualified outcome rather than a raw impression click.
decisionUnit: One ordered set of eligible items for a user or session and surface.
scaleAndConstraints: Large candidate space, online context, cold users/items, bounded latency, and reversible presentation.
successMetrics: Candidate Recall@K, ranker NDCG@K, qualified engagement, hides/complaints, latency, coverage, and concentration.
dataSources: Eligibility, impressions and position, interactions, item metadata, user/session context, inventory state, and policy version.
labeling: Use matured post-exposure outcomes; distinguish unseen items from exposed non-events and correct for position where feasible.
datasetPlan: Build point-in-time examples by user/time; retain natural evaluation prevalence and cold-start slices.
features: User history, item attributes, freshness, request context, and versioned embeddings with availability and cost budgets.
baseline: Popular eligible items by context/recency, then a simple content or collaborative baseline.
modelDiscussion: Add retrieval, a richer ranker, and policy reranking only when each stage earns measurable improvement.
training: Version examples, negatives, features, code, evaluation, and artifact; retrain when catalog or behavior evidence warrants.
offlineArchitecture: Validated events → point-in-time examples → retrieval/ranking training → separate evaluation → versioned model and index.
onlineArchitecture: Request context → eligibility → multi-source retrieval → rank → rerank/policy → response → exposure logging.
evaluation: Measure retrieval recall separately from ordering; inspect cold-user, cold-item, major slice, and concentration errors.
serving: Precompute safe candidates or embeddings, rank online with bounded feature reads, and preserve eligibility after every stage.
capacityReliability: Bound retrieval fan-out, ranker candidates, feature deadlines, cache keys, and fallback capacity.
rollout: Shadow the new path, canary a small eligible share, then experiment on product outcomes with rollback guardrails.
monitoring: Track candidate counts, feature freshness, index/model versions, score distributions, p99 latency, fallback, outcomes, and concentration.
feedbackLoop: Log exposure and propensity; use bounded exploration or diversity policy to avoid self-reinforcing popularity.
responsibleMl: Minimize sensitive signals; evaluate harms and exposure by relevant slice; keep safety and eligibility outside unconstrained ranking.
failureModes: Retriever misses strong items, index is stale, feature outage produces silent defaults, or objective rewards clickbait.
tradeoffs: Freshness versus precomputation, complexity versus debuggability, and personalization versus privacy/cold-start robustness.
alternatives: Use curated, popularity, or contextual rules when data and incremental value do not justify personalization.
extensions: How would session intent, exploration, or multi-objective reranking change the design?
seniorExtensions: Plan encoder/index migration, long-term effects, multi-region ownership, ecosystem incentives, fairness, and cost.
interviewChecklist: Defined surface, eligibility, decision, and baseline.
Separated retrieval, ranking, and policy.
Covered exposure-aware labels, serving, fallback, rollout, and feedback.

title: Social / Content Feed Ranking
summary: Rank rapidly changing content while balancing session relevance, recency, quality, diversity, abuse, and ecosystem effects.
prompt: Design a ranked content feed for a social product with fresh inventory and creator/user ecosystem constraints.
clarifyingQuestions: Is inventory fan-out-on-write, fan-out-on-read, or hybrid, and what is the freshness target?
Which actions, creators, content classes, and safety policies are eligible?
productGoal: Help users find timely, useful content without rewarding low-quality engagement or collapsing creator diversity.
predictionTarget: Order eligible feed candidates for session value under recency, quality, diversity, and safety constraints.
decisionUnit: One ranked page or continuation of a feed for a user session.
scaleAndConstraints: High write/read volume, short-lived inventory, session context, strict latency, network effects, and abuse.
successMetrics: NDCG or calibrated utility offline; satisfied sessions online; hides, complaints, latency, diversity, and creator concentration as guardrails.
dataSources: Candidate source, impressions/position, session events, follows, content/creator metadata, policy results, and freshness.
labeling: Use exposure-aware, time-windowed outcomes and avoid equating dwell or click with satisfaction.
datasetPlan: Temporal user-grouped splits with policy/version context, new-content slices, and abuse-event maturation.
features: Session intent, relationship signals, content/creator quality, freshness, context, and bounded aggregates.
baseline: Reverse-chronological eligible posts from followed creators with simple quality filters.
modelDiscussion: Start with linear or tree ranking; add representation and sequence models only for measured residual problems.
training: Build time-aware examples, preserve exposure policy, and isolate fast-changing features from durable representations.
offlineArchitecture: Feed/exposure events → label maturation → temporal examples → ranker evaluation → artifact registry.
onlineArchitecture: Follow/content candidate sources → freshness/eligibility → rank → diversity/safety policy → feed → exposure logging.
evaluation: Evaluate ordering, freshness, cold creator/user, safety, and concentration; do not rely on short-term engagement alone.
serving: Use hybrid fan-out, cached candidate pools, online session features, bounded reranking, and chronological fallback.
capacityReliability: Bound fan-in per source, hot-celebrity load, session state, feature deadlines, and degradation to safe chronological results.
rollout: Shadow and canary technical behavior; experiment by stable user or cluster where network effects are understood.
monitoring: Track source mix, freshness, concentration, safety actions, score/output shifts, latency, and delayed satisfaction.
feedbackLoop: Model how ranking changes exposure and creator behavior; use bounded exploration and long-term ecosystem measures.
responsibleMl: Keep policy enforcement separable; monitor subgroup and creator effects, abuse adaptation, appeals, and crisis modes.
failureModes: Fresh content never enters candidates, engagement proxy rewards outrage, or a popular creator overloads fan-out.
tradeoffs: Freshness versus compute, personalization versus diversity, and short-term engagement versus ecosystem health.
alternatives: Chronological or lightly scored feeds can be preferable for small networks or high-transparency products.
extensions: How would stories, short video, or breaking-news incidents change the path?
seniorExtensions: Address creator incentives, interference, multi-region feed state, policy migrations, and incident fallbacks.
interviewChecklist: Separated candidate supply, ranking, and policy.
Handled freshness, exposure, concentration, and abuse.
Named chronological fallback and ecosystem-aware rollout.

title: Search Ranking & Retrieval
summary: Combine lexical and learned retrieval with query understanding, ranking, permissions, freshness, and honest fallback.
prompt: Design search ranking and retrieval for a large corpus where permissions and index freshness matter.
clarifyingQuestions: What corpus, query classes, languages, permissions, and freshness targets matter?
Is the goal navigation, fact finding, discovery, or conversion?
productGoal: Return useful, permitted results quickly while preserving exact-match and zero-result recovery.
predictionTarget: Retrieve a high-recall permitted candidate set, then order it for task relevance and quality.
decisionUnit: An ordered result set for one normalized query and search context.
scaleAndConstraints: Large corpus, per-query latency, permissions, index updates, rare queries, and biased click feedback.
successMetrics: Recall@K for retrieval, MRR/NDCG@K for ranking, task completion, reformulation, zero-result rate, permission failures, and latency.
dataSources: Corpus/version, query and result exposure, clicks/actions, reformulations, judgments, permissions, and index state.
labeling: Combine explicit judgments and exposure-aware behavior; treat position and presentation as bias.
datasetPlan: Time-aware query splits with head/tail, locale, permission, and fresh-document slices plus hard negatives.
features: Lexical match, field quality, freshness, query/document representations, context, and permission eligibility.
baseline: Inverted index with BM25-style lexical retrieval, normalization, filters, and deterministic ranking signals.
modelDiscussion: Add semantic retrieval and learned ranking only for measured recall or ordering gaps; keep stage metrics separate.
training: Version judgments, click-policy context, encoders, lexical configuration, and index-compatible artifacts.
offlineArchitecture: Corpus + judgments/exposures → lexical/semantic training → retrieval and ranking evaluation → model/index versions.
onlineArchitecture: Query normalization → lexical + semantic retrieval → merge → lightweight rank → rerank → permissions/policy → results.
evaluation: Measure retrieval misses, ranking errors, fresh and tail queries, permissions, and zero-result diagnosis separately.
serving: Parallelize retrieval branches, enforce permissions throughout, cap reranking depth, and preserve lexical fallback.
capacityReliability: Budget query understanding, fan-out, index reads, reranking, and cache; isolate index or model failure.
rollout: Build a parallel index, shadow queries, canary compatible model/index pairs, and experiment only after relevance/safety gates.
monitoring: Track query mix, zero results, candidate counts, index lag, permission filtering, latency, fallback, and outcomes.
feedbackLoop: Log displayed ranks and counter position bias; avoid learning only from current retriever exposure.
responsibleMl: Treat access control as a hard constraint, minimize query retention, and monitor unsafe or sensitive result classes.
failureModes: Best document never enters candidates, stale index omits updates, or permission revocation lags a semantic index.
tradeoffs: Recall versus latency, lexical transparency versus semantic generalization, and freshness versus index cost.
alternatives: Lexical search alone is often sufficient for exact terms, identifiers, small corpora, or strict transparency.
extensions: How would federated, cross-lingual, hybrid, or multimodal search change retrieval?
seniorExtensions: Design adaptive depth, index migrations, permission revocation, regional placement, and multi-tenant cost isolation.
interviewChecklist: Defined corpus, task, permissions, and lexical baseline.
Separated retrieval recall from ranking quality.
Handled index compatibility, freshness, exposure bias, and fallback.

title: Autocomplete & Query Suggestions
summary: Serve safe, fresh prefix suggestions within an every-keystroke latency budget.
prompt: Design autocomplete and query suggestions for a global search product.
clarifyingQuestions: Which locales, surfaces, personalization, and unsafe suggestion policies apply?
What p99 budget and update cadence must hold per keystroke?
productGoal: Reduce typing and guide users toward useful, safe queries without distorting intent.
predictionTarget: Rank eligible completions for a prefix, locale, session, and optional user context.
decisionUnit: A short ordered suggestion list for one prefix event.
scaleAndConstraints: Every-keystroke QPS, tiny latency budget, unseen prefixes, trends, locale, safety, and cacheability.
successMetrics: Accepted useful suggestions, keystrokes saved, abandonment/reformulation, unsafe suggestion rate, coverage, and p99 latency.
dataSources: Prefix exposures, selected suggestion, final submitted query, locale/session, trend counts, and safety decisions.
labeling: Selection is an implicit label with position bias; final query and downstream task outcome provide stronger context.
datasetPlan: Temporal prefix splits with head/tail and locale slices; keep unsafe examples for policy evaluation, not serving.
features: Prefix match, normalized popularity, recency/trend, locale, session context, and safety classification.
baseline: Trie or FST over eligible popular queries with normalization, locale partitioning, and block rules.
modelDiscussion: Add learned reranking or generation only when unseen-prefix or personalization value justifies latency and safety risk.
training: Aggregate exposure-aware counts, validate spikes, train optional ranker, and version candidate and safety policies.
offlineArchitecture: Query/exposure logs → validation + aggregation → prefix index and optional ranker → safety evaluation → versioned publish.
onlineArchitecture: Prefix → normalize/locale → cache → prefix candidates → rank → safety policy → suggestions → exposure log.
evaluation: Inspect head/tail prefixes, locale, trend spikes, harmful suggestions, coverage, and latency under rapid typing.
serving: Edge/cache hot prefixes, bound candidate work, debounce or cancel obsolete requests, and return safe popularity fallback.
capacityReliability: Plan burst QPS, cache hit rate, cancellation, regional indices, and empty-safe response when policy is unavailable.
rollout: Shadow candidate changes, canary by locale or user, and block on safety, latency, or query-shift guardrails.
monitoring: Track prefix volume, cache hit, index freshness, unsafe blocks, accepted suggestions, empty rate, and p99 latency.
feedbackLoop: Presentation increases suggestion popularity; retain exposure and use bounded trend logic to prevent runaway amplification.
responsibleMl: Filter harassment, self-harm, sexual, violent, and sensitive personal suggestions using product policy and human escalation.
failureModes: Trend poisoning, unsafe suggestions, cache stampede, stale locale data, or obsolete responses arriving out of order.
tradeoffs: Fresh trends versus manipulation, personalization versus privacy/cacheability, and coverage versus safety.
alternatives: A non-personalized popularity prefix index is often the right first system.
extensions: How would zero-result diagnosis or spelling correction share signals without coupling releases?
seniorExtensions: Plan locale isolation, incident kill switches, adversarial trend response, versioned client behavior, and load spikes.
interviewChecklist: Started with trie/FST popularity baseline.
Budgeted every-keystroke latency and cancellation.
Handled exposure bias, trend abuse, locale, safety, and fallback.

title: Ads Retrieval & Ranking
summary: Retrieve eligible ads and combine calibrated predictions with pacing, value, auction policy, and user guardrails.
prompt: Design ad retrieval and ranking for a large marketplace with delayed conversions and budget constraints.
clarifyingQuestions: Which surface, auction boundary, advertiser objective, billing event, and user policy apply?
How delayed are conversions and how strict are budget/pacing guarantees?
productGoal: Deliver useful eligible ads while protecting users, advertiser value, budgets, and platform health.
predictionTarget: Estimate calibrated click/conversion value for an eligible impression; policy and auction determine the final action.
decisionUnit: One eligible ad slate or winner for an impression opportunity.
scaleAndConstraints: Huge inventory, low latency, budgets, pacing, delayed labels, attribution, competing objectives, and policy eligibility.
successMetrics: Retrieval recall, log loss/calibration, ranking utility, incremental outcomes, spend/budget accuracy, latency, complaints, and advertiser concentration.
dataSources: Eligibility, bids/value inputs, impressions/positions, clicks, conversions, attribution state, budgets, pacing, and policy decisions.
labeling: Use exposure and maturation windows for clicks/conversions; version attribution and distinguish prediction from auction outcome.
datasetPlan: Point-in-time impression examples with delayed-label updates, advertiser/campaign splits, and natural-prevalence evaluation.
features: Query/context, ad/advertiser quality, campaign state, user context where allowed, historical aggregates, and calibration segments.
baseline: Eligible ads ordered by a transparent value/quality rule with budget and pacing constraints.
modelDiscussion: Add calibrated pCTR/pCVR and learned ranking; keep auction, policy, and pacing as explicit separable components.
training: Version attribution, matured labels, sampled negatives, calibration, feature snapshots, and artifact/policy compatibility.
offlineArchitecture: Exposure + conversion logs → maturation/attribution → examples → calibrated predictors/ranker → evaluation + registry.
onlineArchitecture: Opportunity → eligibility → retrieval → calibrated predictions → policy/pacing/auction → ad → exposure log.
evaluation: Evaluate calibration and ranking by campaign, surface, region, value band, and maturity; separate observational revenue from causal lift.
serving: Bound retrieval/ranking, keep current budgets and eligibility authoritative, and fall back to safe house/no-ad or transparent ranking.
capacityReliability: Plan hot campaigns, budget update lag, regional serving, duplicate spend protection, and decision deadlines.
rollout: Shadow predictions, canary serving behavior, and use controlled experiments for user/product impact where interference is acceptable.
monitoring: Track calibration, spend/pacing, eligible counts, latency, stale budgets, complaints, concentration, and delayed conversions.
feedbackLoop: Ranking changes exposure and future advertiser data; monitor marketplace concentration and attribution feedback.
responsibleMl: Enforce ad policy and sensitive-category controls outside unconstrained scoring; preserve audit and advertiser/user recourse.
failureModes: Delayed conversion mislabeled negative, stale budget overspends, miscalibration distorts value, or policy filtering occurs too late.
tradeoffs: Revenue versus user experience, freshness versus consistent budget state, and personalization versus privacy.
alternatives: Contextual or rule-based ads may be preferable where personalization evidence or consent is insufficient.
extensions: How would brand ads, conversion ads, or geo experiments change evaluation?
seniorExtensions: Address interference, attribution, advertiser fairness, auction/model co-design, regional consistency, and long-term user effects.
interviewChecklist: Separated eligibility, prediction, pacing, policy, and auction.
Handled delayed conversions and calibration.
Covered budgets, causal validation, guardrails, and fallbacks.

title: Real-Time Payment Fraud
summary: Score rare adversarial transactions with streaming features, calibrated action bands, review, appeals, and safe fallback.
prompt: Design a real-time payment fraud decision system under strict latency and asymmetric intervention costs.
clarifyingQuestions: Which payment stage and actions—allow, challenge, review, block—are in scope?
What are latency, chargeback delay, review capacity, reversal, and audit constraints?
productGoal: Reduce confirmed fraud loss without unacceptable false blocks, friction, or reviewer overload.
predictionTarget: Estimate transaction risk for policy action; do not treat the score itself as enforcement.
decisionUnit: One transaction authorization or post-authorization review decision.
scaleAndConstraints: Rare positives, adversarial adaptation, delayed/disputed labels, strict p99, streaming features, and asymmetric harm.
successMetrics: Precision/recall and PR-AUC, calibrated loss, fraud loss, false-block/step-up rates, review capacity, appeal reversals, and p99 latency.
dataSources: Transaction, account/device/merchant context, velocity events, prior actions, chargebacks, disputes, review outcomes, and policy version.
labeling: Keep chargebacks pending through maturation; preserve disputes, reversals, reviewer source, and policy changes.
datasetPlan: Temporal entity-aware splits, point-in-time velocity joins, natural prevalence, attack-era slices, and leakage audits.
features: Transaction context, entity reputation, device signals, graph/velocity aggregates, and missing/stale indicators.
baseline: Auditable rules for known high-risk patterns plus allow/challenge/review policy.
modelDiscussion: Start with calibrated linear/tree models; add graph or representation signals only for measured coordinated-attack gaps.
training: Version label maturity, sampling, point-in-time features, attack periods, calibration, and action-policy compatibility.
offlineArchitecture: Transactions + disputes/reviews → label maturation → point-in-time examples → train/calibrate → policy simulation → registry.
onlineArchitecture: Payment request + streaming features → scorer → action bands → allow/challenge/review/block → audit + outcome logging.
evaluation: Evaluate natural prevalence, loss-weighted operating points, calibration, new-attack and subgroup slices, and reviewer queues.
serving: Parallel bounded feature reads and rules/model scoring; degrade to risk-appropriate rules or challenge, never silent unsafe defaults.
capacityReliability: Budget feature and inference latency, bound review queue, isolate providers, and define regional consistency/failover.
rollout: Replay and shadow first, canary low-risk traffic, cap actions, monitor false positives and latency, then widen with instant rollback.
monitoring: Track feature quality, score/action bands, p99, fallback, review backlog, chargebacks, appeals, and attack segments.
feedbackLoop: Fraudsters adapt and policy changes observed data; retain rules/model versions and controlled exploration only where safe.
responsibleMl: Limit sensitive data, audit high-impact actions, explain review inputs appropriately, and support human review and appeal.
failureModes: Feature outage defaults to low risk, delayed labels poison negatives, review queue overloads, or attacker shifts entities.
tradeoffs: Fraud loss versus false-block harm, freshness versus latency, and review depth versus capacity.
alternatives: Rules plus step-up verification may outperform ML where labels are scarce or policy is stable.
extensions: How would account takeover, coordinated graph attacks, or cross-border traffic change the system?
seniorExtensions: Design graph signals, multi-region state, policy migrations, adversarial response, audit, and degraded feature modes.
interviewChecklist: Defined actions, costs, latency, and rule baseline.
Handled rare delayed labels, calibration, and review capacity.
Covered safe fallback, adversaries, audit, and appeal.

title: Trust & Safety Decision System
summary: Separate detection from policy, human review, enforcement, appeal, and evolving adversarial response.
prompt: Design a trust and safety decision system for harmful content or account behavior.
clarifyingQuestions: Which policy taxonomy, content modalities, actions, appeal rights, locales, and crisis modes apply?
Which decisions may be automated versus reviewed?
productGoal: Reduce defined harm while preserving policy consistency, user recourse, reviewer safety, and legitimate expression.
predictionTarget: Estimate policy-relevant signals; a separate policy layer chooses review or enforcement.
decisionUnit: One content/account event and its policy action, with linked review and appeal state.
scaleAndConstraints: Disputed labels, multimodal content, evolving adversaries, locale context, review capacity, audit, and high-impact actions.
successMetrics: Policy-class precision/recall, severity-weighted misses, appeal reversal, reviewer agreement/backlog, exposure to harm, and latency.
dataSources: Content/event, reports, exposure, policy taxonomy/version, automated signals, reviewer decisions, escalations, and appeals.
labeling: Preserve policy version, reviewer/adjudicator context, disagreement, reversals, and unknown or ambiguous states.
datasetPlan: Time/policy-aware splits with locale, severity, new-abuse, and appeal slices; prevent near-duplicate leakage.
features: Content/account/network signals with strict access and minimization; make missing modalities explicit.
baseline: Policy rules, known-block lists, rate limits, and human review for ambiguous high-impact cases.
modelDiscussion: Use cascades or specialized detectors only where labeled evidence and policy boundaries support them.
training: Version taxonomy, reviewer guidance, data access, label provenance, model, thresholds, and escalation policy.
offlineArchitecture: Reports/reviews/appeals → adjudicated policy labels → slice evaluation → accepted detector artifacts.
onlineArchitecture: Content/event → rules/detectors → policy mapping → allow/limit/review/enforce → notice/appeal → audit.
evaluation: Weight severe misses and wrongful actions; inspect locale, group, abuse type, reviewer agreement, and appeal outcomes.
serving: Use staged cascades, bounded review queues, policy kill switches, and fail-safe behavior when critical evidence is missing.
capacityReliability: Plan incident spikes, reviewer capacity, queue priorities, dependency isolation, and crisis-mode policy.
rollout: Replay and shadow, canary non-enforcement signals, require human confirmation for early high-impact actions, and retain rollback.
monitoring: Track class/slice errors, review backlog, appeals, policy drift, data quality, adversarial shifts, and enforcement incidents.
feedbackLoop: Enforcement changes attacker behavior and observed examples; maintain red-team, appeal, and incident feedback without blindly retraining.
responsibleMl: Apply minimization, reviewer protections, notice, appeal, auditability, and accountable policy ownership throughout.
failureModes: Model output becomes policy, reviewer labels are treated as objective truth, or appeal cannot correct future data.
tradeoffs: Automation speed versus review quality, detection recall versus wrongful action, and global consistency versus locale context.
alternatives: Keep ambiguous or high-impact cases human-led when evidence and reversibility are insufficient.
extensions: How would spam, crisis events, coordinated abuse, or multimodal content change the cascade?
seniorExtensions: Design taxonomy migration, reviewer quality, cross-locale governance, crisis response, audit, and adversarial adaptation.
interviewChecklist: Separated model estimate, policy, review, enforcement, and appeal.
Versioned disputed labels and taxonomy.
Covered adversaries, reviewer capacity, audit, and crisis fallback.

title: ETA Prediction
summary: Correct a strong routing baseline with fresh spatiotemporal signals while protecting tail error and fallback.
prompt: Design ETA prediction for a routing or delivery product with live traffic and regional variation.
clarifyingQuestions: Is the ETA pre-trip, in-trip, courier arrival, or delivery completion, and at what horizon?
What update frequency, tail-error tolerance, and routing dependency apply?
productGoal: Provide useful, stable arrival expectations that improve planning without misleading users.
predictionTarget: Predict remaining or total duration, optionally quantiles, relative to a route/domain baseline.
decisionUnit: One route/trip at a defined observation time and horizon.
scaleAndConstraints: Low latency, live traffic, location noise, regional/map drift, changing routes, and asymmetric early/late errors.
successMetrics: MAE/RMSE, percentile and quantile coverage, error by region/horizon/traffic, user correction behavior, p99 latency, and stability.
dataSources: Route baseline, map/version, historical trip segments, live traffic, location/time/weather context where justified, and completion timestamps.
labeling: Define start/end and paused/cancelled cases; version route/map context and avoid post-arrival signals.
datasetPlan: Temporal and regional splits with peak/off-peak, incident, route-change, and rare-tail slices.
features: Route baseline, distance/segment, time, live traffic, recent regional speed, vehicle/order context, and freshness indicators.
baseline: Routing engine or historical segment-time estimate before learned correction.
modelDiscussion: Use regression or quantile models for residual correction; add sequence/graph complexity only for measured route interactions.
training: Build point-in-time trip snapshots and labels, version maps/routes, evaluate horizons, and publish compatible correction models.
offlineArchitecture: Trips + route/map versions → point-in-time snapshots → baseline residual/quantile training → regional/horizon evaluation.
onlineArchitecture: Route baseline + live context → feature freshness gate → correction model → interval/policy → ETA response + outcome log.
evaluation: Inspect tail, calibration/coverage, region, horizon, traffic regime, new-road, and incident errors—not one global MAE.
serving: Compute route first, fetch bounded fresh context, apply lightweight correction, and fall back to the route baseline.
capacityReliability: Budget map/routing dependency, feature reads, model latency, update rate, regional cache, and stale-traffic behavior.
rollout: Shadow against live trips, canary by region, compare error/stability and latency, then widen with baseline rollback.
monitoring: Track feature/map freshness, ETA distribution, residuals when trips complete, coverage, regional slices, latency, and fallback.
feedbackLoop: Routing and user behavior react to ETA; distinguish policy-induced route changes from model error.
responsibleMl: Minimize precise location retention and restrict access; communicate uncertainty without false precision.
failureModes: Map version mismatch, stale traffic, GPS jumps, route changes, incident regimes, or unstable ETA updates.
tradeoffs: Freshness versus latency, stable communication versus frequent correction, and one model versus regional specialization.
alternatives: A calibrated routing baseline may be sufficient where residual gains are small or data is sparse.
extensions: How would fleet assignment, multi-stop delivery, or route-policy changes affect labels?
seniorExtensions: Address regional drift, map migrations, uncertainty, incident modes, fleet cost, and route/model interaction.
interviewChecklist: Defined horizon and routing baseline.
Used temporal/regional evaluation and uncertainty.
Covered freshness, route changes, privacy, and baseline fallback.

title: Demand Forecasting
summary: Produce multi-horizon forecast distributions with rolling validation and operational cost awareness.
prompt: Design demand forecasting for inventory or staffing decisions across products and regions.
clarifyingQuestions: What entity, granularity, horizon, decision cadence, and downstream cost define demand?
How do promotions, holidays, stockouts, substitutions, and new items affect observed demand?
productGoal: Support inventory or staffing decisions with useful uncertainty and asymmetric cost awareness.
predictionTarget: Forecast demand distribution by entity, location, interval, and horizon—not merely one point estimate.
decisionUnit: One forecast distribution for an entity/location/horizon consumed by an operational decision.
scaleAndConstraints: Many related series, seasonality, promotions, censored demand, hierarchy, batch deadlines, and rare events.
successMetrics: MAE/RMSE or scale-aware error, quantile loss and coverage, bias, slice/horizon metrics, stockout/waste/staffing cost, freshness, and batch completion.
dataSources: Historical demand, prices/promotions, inventory/stockout state, calendar, location, product hierarchy, weather/events where justified, and decisions.
labeling: Define demand versus observed sales; flag stockout censoring, returns, cancellations, and late corrections.
datasetPlan: Use rolling-origin validation across several cutoffs, realistic horizons, entity cold-start, and event/season slices.
features: Lags, rolling aggregates, seasonality, calendar, promotion, hierarchy, availability, and known-future covariates only.
baseline: Seasonal naive or moving-average forecast at the required granularity and horizon.
modelDiscussion: Progress from statistical or tree baselines to global/deep forecasting only when cross-series evidence justifies it.
training: Build cutoff-aware datasets, run rolling backtests, register forecast/config versions, and publish only after cost and calibration gates.
offlineArchitecture: Historical signals → cutoff snapshots → rolling backtests → point/quantile forecasts → reconciliation → artifact.
onlineArchitecture: Scheduled batch → forecast store → downstream inventory/staffing policy → realized/censored outcomes → corrections.
evaluation: Evaluate every horizon, hierarchy level, high/low volume segment, cold start, promotion, stockout, and rare-event period.
serving: Publish versioned batch forecasts before the decision deadline; expose freshness and fall back to seasonal naive estimates.
capacityReliability: Plan series count × horizons × backtests, deadline, retry, partial publication, and downstream version compatibility.
rollout: Backtest first, shadow downstream decisions, canary selected regions/categories, and compare operational cost before wider use.
monitoring: Track batch freshness/completion, forecast distribution, bias, interval coverage, censored outcomes, cost, and regime slices.
feedbackLoop: Inventory and pricing decisions change observed sales; retain stockout and policy context to avoid learning censored demand as true demand.
responsibleMl: Review resource-allocation harms and do not use sensitive proxies without justified need and controls.
failureModes: Random split leakage, stockouts treated as low demand, missing promotion data, hierarchy inconsistency, or missed batch deadline.
tradeoffs: Granularity versus variance/cost, responsiveness versus stability, and point accuracy versus calibrated uncertainty.
alternatives: Seasonal naive forecasts can be operationally superior when data is sparse, stable, or downstream decisions are simple.
extensions: How would new-item cold start, nowcasting, rare events, or optimization coupling change the design?
seniorExtensions: Design hierarchical reconciliation, scenario overrides, rare-event operations, causal promotion treatment, and ownership.
interviewChecklist: Defined entity, horizon, decision, and seasonal baseline.
Used rolling-origin evaluation and uncertainty.
Handled censoring, batch deadlines, operational cost, and fallback.

title: Feature Store
summary: Design a shared temporal feature platform only when reuse, point-in-time correctness, and online delivery earn it.
prompt: Design a feature store for multiple teams that need historical training retrieval and low-latency online features.
clarifyingQuestions: Who are the users, how many features/models, and which historical and online latency/freshness needs exist?
Why is a shared platform better than versioned pipeline-local features?
productGoal: Make reusable features correct, discoverable, owned, and consistently deliverable without hiding temporal semantics.
predictionTarget: This is infrastructure: define platform service outcomes, not a fake prediction target.
decisionUnit: A feature definition and its historical or online value for an entity at a specific event time.
scaleAndConstraints: Many tenants/features, historical volume, online QPS/latency, materialization freshness, backfills, governance, and regional placement.
successMetrics: Point-in-time correctness, training-serving skew, online p99/availability, freshness, backfill completion, adoption/reuse, cost, and incidents.
dataSources: Versioned definitions, entities, event timestamps, batch/stream sources, transformations, ownership, lineage, and access policy.
labeling: No labels are required for the platform itself; consumer models retain label ownership and joins.
datasetPlan: Historical retrieval accepts entity/event-time frames and returns auditable point-in-time values with source versions.
features: Registry metadata, offline history, online materialization, freshness, defaults, owners, and deprecation state.
baseline: Versioned transformations inside each model pipeline plus a simple online key-value store where necessary.
modelDiscussion: Do not introduce a model; the design problem is temporal data infrastructure.
training: Consumer pipelines retrieve historical features by event time and record definition/data versions in lineage.
offlineArchitecture: Sources → validated transformations → offline feature history → point-in-time retrieval → consumer dataset.
onlineArchitecture: Sources/streams → materialization → online store → low-latency feature service → consumer model.
evaluation: Test temporal correctness, parity, replay, skew, defaults, freshness, backfills, and tenant isolation.
serving: Shard by entity/access pattern, use explicit TTL/freshness, isolate tenants, and return visible stale/missing state.
capacityReliability: Plan storage history, hot entities, online QPS, stream lag, backfill isolation, quotas, and regional failover.
rollout: Migrate one feature/model pair, dual-read and compare, backfill safely, then expand with rollback and deprecation windows.
monitoring: Track materialization lag, skew, missing/default rates, p99, store errors, backfill impact, ownership, and cost.
feedbackLoop: Measure whether reuse and incidents improve; avoid platform expansion based only on feature count.
responsibleMl: Enforce least privilege, purpose metadata, retention, sensitive-feature review, audit, and tenant isolation.
failureModes: Latest-value historical joins, hidden stale defaults, backfill overload, orphaned definitions, or cross-tenant access.
tradeoffs: Central consistency versus platform coupling, freshness versus cost, and reuse versus governance burden.
alternatives: Keep pipeline-local features until several teams share real definitions and correctness/serving pain.
extensions: How would batch-only use, multi-region online serving, or feature deprecation change scope?
seniorExtensions: Design multi-tenancy, regional placement, migration, backfill isolation, disaster recovery, and organizational ownership.
interviewChecklist: Justified build-versus-not.
Covered point-in-time history and online materialization.
Handled skew, freshness, backfills, tenancy, governance, and migration.

title: ML Training & Deployment Platform
summary: Coordinate reproducible training, evaluation, registry, promotion, quotas, and scheduled or event-driven operation.
prompt: Design a multi-tenant platform for training, evaluating, registering, and deploying production ML artifacts.
clarifyingQuestions: Which personas, frameworks, data boundaries, workload sizes, and deployment targets must be supported?
What should remain self-service versus centrally governed?
productGoal: Let teams run reproducible learning workflows and promote evidence-backed artifacts safely within resource and governance bounds.
predictionTarget: This is infrastructure: success is reproducible lifecycle execution, not a model score.
decisionUnit: One versioned workflow run and its artifact promotion decision.
scaleAndConstraints: Multi-tenant compute, heterogeneous jobs, quotas, lineage, retries, backfills, secrets/data access, artifacts, and regional failure.
successMetrics: Run success/retry, queue time, reproducibility, artifact lineage completeness, failed promotions, deployment lead time, utilization, cost, and incidents.
dataSources: Workflow definitions, code/config, datasets/features, environments, experiment metadata, artifacts, evaluations, approvals, and deployment state.
labeling: Consumer teams own model labels; the platform validates declared datasets and records lineage.
datasetPlan: Snapshot references and access policy, isolate backfills, and make run inputs immutable or content-addressed.
features: No model features are required; feature platform integration is optional and explicit.
baseline: Repository-defined batch jobs, object storage, CI, and a small registry before a general platform.
modelDiscussion: The platform supports model families without choosing one or forcing GPU use.
training: DAG stages validate data, prepare datasets, train, evaluate, and register accepted artifacts with idempotent retries.
offlineArchitecture: API/control plane → scheduler → isolated compute → data/artifact stores → evaluation → registry/lineage.
onlineArchitecture: Promotion service → deployment adapters → serving targets → health/quality signals → rollback controller.
evaluation: Validate workflow reproducibility, artifact compatibility, security boundaries, failure recovery, and consumer-defined gates.
serving: Keep deployment target adapters separate; require explicit compatibility and observe rollout without owning every runtime.
capacityReliability: Use quotas, priority/preemption, admission, retry budgets, idempotency, backfill pools, durable state, and disaster recovery.
rollout: Onboard one workload family, preserve existing jobs, prove lineage and rollback, then expand tenants and deployment targets.
monitoring: Track queue/run states, utilization, cost, artifact/gate outcomes, deployment health, tenant errors, and control-plane incidents.
feedbackLoop: Use adoption, lead time, failure, and operator burden to decide platform evolution—not feature-request count alone.
responsibleMl: Enforce workload identity, least privilege, secret isolation, data purpose/access, audit, retention, and approval policy.
failureModes: Retries duplicate jobs, mutable data breaks reproducibility, one tenant starves others, or registry promotion bypasses gates.
tradeoffs: Flexibility versus standardization, utilization versus isolation, and self-service speed versus governance.
alternatives: Keep thin orchestration when organization size and workload diversity do not justify a platform.
extensions: How would GPU scheduling, regulated data, edge deployment, or event-driven retraining change the control plane?
seniorExtensions: Design multi-region control state, quota governance, disaster recovery, framework/runtime migrations, and team ownership.
interviewChecklist: Defined personas and a smaller baseline.
Separated control, compute, data/artifact, and deployment planes.
Covered lineage, gates, retries, quotas, isolation, and recovery.

title: Scalable Online Inference Service
summary: Serve a heterogeneous model fleet with explicit SLOs, routing, batching, autoscaling, compatibility, admission, and graceful degradation.
prompt: Design a scalable online inference service for latency-sensitive CPU models and batchable GPU workloads.
clarifyingQuestions: Which model sizes/runtimes, request shapes, p99, throughput, tenancy, regions, and cost targets matter?
Are models dedicated, multi-model, streaming, stateful, or independently deployable?
productGoal: Provide predictable, compatible inference with bounded cost and safe degradation across a model fleet.
predictionTarget: This is infrastructure: preserve each model's declared input/output contract and service SLO.
decisionUnit: One inference request or batch routed to a compatible model/runtime version.
scaleAndConstraints: Tail latency, burst traffic, model loading, CPU/GPU pools, batching, autoscaling lag, tenancy, regions, and cost.
successMetrics: p50/p99 latency, throughput, error/timeout, queue depth, availability, cold starts, fallback, utilization, cost/request, and quality guardrails.
dataSources: Deployment specs, model/runtime artifacts, resource profiles, request metadata, routing state, health, and quality signals.
labeling: Consumer models own labels; service quality joins versioned predictions to delayed consumer outcomes where permitted.
datasetPlan: Use replay/load traces and representative payloads without copying private features into platform analytics.
features: Feature access remains outside or in explicit preprocessors; the service validates schemas and compatibility.
baseline: One stateless service per model on CPU with health checks, replicas, and simple autoscaling.
modelDiscussion: Choose runtime and hardware per measured profile; no universal GPU, batching, or multi-model architecture.
training: Out of scope except artifact/runtime compatibility and evaluation metadata required for promotion.
offlineArchitecture: Artifact registry + benchmarks → deployment spec → capacity profile → staged rollout configuration.
onlineArchitecture: Gateway → admission/routing → preprocess → CPU/GPU model pool → postprocess → response + versioned telemetry.
evaluation: Load-test realistic shapes and concurrency; verify numerical/schema compatibility, quality equivalence, saturation, and fallback.
serving: Separate control/data plane, route by version/runtime, batch where latency permits, preload or cache models, and bound queues.
capacityReliability: Plan warm capacity, autoscaling signals/lag, admission, load shedding, pool isolation, regional failover, and disaster recovery.
rollout: Register compatible runtime/model, shadow, canary by weighted traffic, compare per-version quality/performance, then promote or rollback.
monitoring: Track per-version latency, queue, resource saturation, errors, cold starts, cache, fallback, cost, and consumer quality.
feedbackLoop: Use workload and incident evidence to revise profiles and capacity; avoid autoscaling solely on CPU for GPU/queue-bound work.
responsibleMl: Isolate tenants, redact payload telemetry, enforce model access, audit deployments, and prevent cross-tenant cache leakage.
failureModes: Queue explosion, cold-start storm, GPU fragmentation, incompatible runtime, noisy neighbor, or regional dependency outage.
tradeoffs: Batching throughput versus latency, warm capacity versus cost, and shared pools versus isolation.
alternatives: Dedicated services remain simpler for small fleets or strong isolation requirements.
extensions: How would multi-model GPU serving, token streaming, edge inference, or regional failover change routing?
seniorExtensions: Design tenant isolation, GPU fragmentation control, regional capacity, runtime migration, and cost governance.
interviewChecklist: Defined SLO, workload classes, and dedicated baseline.
Budgeted queueing, batching, loading, autoscaling, and admission.
Covered compatibility, tenancy, rollout, cost, and fallback.

title: Production RAG / Enterprise AI Assistant
summary: Join permission-aware retrieval and generation with separate evaluation, citations, injection controls, cost, and fallback.
prompt: Design a production retrieval-augmented assistant over an enterprise corpus with changing permissions.
clarifyingQuestions: Which tasks, corpus, freshness, permissions, citations, actions, quality bar, and human handoff are required?
What happens when evidence is missing, conflicting, malicious, or too expensive to retrieve?
productGoal: Help users complete bounded knowledge tasks with accessible evidence while protecting permissions, privacy, and safe fallback.
predictionTarget: Retrieve useful permitted evidence and generate a response grounded in that context; evaluate the stages separately.
decisionUnit: One query/session producing retrieved evidence, answer, citations, and optional tool/action decision.
scaleAndConstraints: Corpus ingestion/freshness, ACL changes, retrieval recall, model variability, context budget, latency/cost, injection, and audit.
successMetrics: Retrieval Recall@K, citation/evidence coverage, answer task quality, unsupported-claim rate, refusal/handoff quality, permissions, p99, and cost.
dataSources: Versioned corpus, ownership/ACLs, ingestion state, queries, retrieved passages, citations, feedback, evaluator judgments, and incidents.
labeling: Separate retrieval relevance, evidence support, answer usefulness, safety, and task completion labels with evaluator provenance.
datasetPlan: Build permission-safe evaluation sets with fresh/stale, unanswerable, conflicting, adversarial, and major task slices.
features: Lexical/dense retrieval signals, metadata, access context, reranking, query/session state, and source freshness.
baseline: Permission-filtered keyword search with cited snippets or a no-answer handoff.
modelDiscussion: Add dense retrieval, reranking, and generation only where each stage improves a measured task; avoid one-model claims.
training: Version chunking, corpus/index, embeddings, reranker, prompt/policy, generator, evaluation set, and tool contracts.
offlineArchitecture: Sources + ACLs → validate/chunk → sparse/dense indexes → eval retrieval/rerank/generation → compatible versions.
onlineArchitecture: Query + identity → permission-aware retrieve → rerank → context construction → generate/cite → policy/tool/handoff → audit.
evaluation: Measure retrieval before generation; inspect evidence support, unanswerable behavior, permissions, injection, latency, and cost.
serving: Parallel safe retrieval, bounded context, model routing/caching where valid, timeouts, citation construction, and search-only or human fallback.
capacityReliability: Budget retrieval, rerank, context, generation, tool calls, rate limits, queues, and provider/region degradation.
rollout: Offline adversarial/evidence gates, shadow, internal canary, bounded user tasks, monitored expansion, and reversible model/index/prompt sets.
monitoring: Track index/ACL freshness, retrieval depth, unsupported answers, refusals, injection attempts, p99, cost, fallback, and task outcomes.
feedbackLoop: Keep user feedback distinct from truth; route corrections to corpus owners and evaluation before retraining or prompt changes.
responsibleMl: Enforce access before and after retrieval, treat retrieved text as untrusted, minimize logs, show citations, and preserve escalation/audit.
failureModes: ACL revocation lags index, retriever misses evidence, prompt injection redirects behavior, citation is decorative, or model invents unsupported claims.
tradeoffs: Recall versus context/cost, freshness versus indexing load, helpfulness versus abstention, and personalization versus privacy.
alternatives: Permission-filtered search or curated workflows are better when generation adds little task value or unacceptable uncertainty.
extensions: How would tool use, multimodal sources, multilingual retrieval, or regulated data change the design?
seniorExtensions: Design multi-tenancy, ACL revocation, model/index/prompt migration, evaluation governance, tool isolation, and incident containment.
interviewChecklist: Defined task, corpus, permission, and search baseline.
Separated retrieval, reranking, generation, and evaluation.
Covered ACL freshness, injection, citations, cost, fallback, and version coupling.
